A machine learning case study by Timur

100 people left the hospital today. 11 of them will be back within a month.

Hospitals try to stop that with something surprisingly simple, a phone call in the first few days at home, but there's never enough time to call everyone. So I built an AI to decide who gets the call, put it head to head against a nurse's instincts, and ended up finding out where AI really belongs in this job, which turned out to be somewhere I didn't expect.

16 min readPython · SQL · PyTorch · LLMsBuilt in 2026

Act one

Why one phone call mattersand why there's never time to make them all

Leaving the hospital feels like the finish line, but for a lot of patients it's where things quietly start to go wrong. Picture an older woman who was admitted because her heart wasn't pumping well. She goes home with a bag of new prescriptions, a couple of appointments she's supposed to book, and a printed sheet of warning signs, and she's expected to manage all of it on her own while she's still tired and a little foggy from the stay.

Here's how the next month can go, depending on whether someone picks up the phone and checks in on her.

One month at home, two ways

An illustrative example to show the idea, not a real patient.

This happens often enough that it has a name, a 30-day readmission, which simply means coming back into the hospital within a month of leaving it. Hospitals watch that number closely for three reasons: it's bad for the patient, it fills beds that other people need, and in the United States the government's Medicare program fines hospitals that have too many of them.

One of the simplest ways to prevent it is exactly that phone call. Many hospitals have nurses, usually called care managers, whose job includes calling patients a few days after they get home to make sure they've picked up their prescriptions, know when their next appointment is, and understand which symptoms mean they should call the doctor instead of waiting it out.

A short phone call in the first few days at home can catch a small problem before it turns into another hospital stay.

The catch: you can't call everyone

A hospital can send home dozens or even hundreds of people in a single day, and each careful call takes time, so a care manager simply can't reach all of them. To keep things concrete, I used a simple version of that situation throughout this project: 100 patients go home each day, and there's time to call 20 of them. That means every morning somebody has to decide which 20 people get a call, and which 80 are on their own.

Today that decision mostly comes from experience. Nurses learn that the patients most likely to come back tend to be the ones who've been in the hospital a lot before, who are older, who have several long-term conditions, or who went home with complicated medication changes, and some hospitals turn a few of those facts into a quick checklist score. It works reasonably well. Still, it's a quick judgment made under time pressure every single morning, and that's exactly the kind of decision people are now trying to hand over to AI.

Every morning in this project
20 people get a call80 people are on their ownAbout 11 of the 100 will be back within a month, and nobody knows which ones yet
So the question behind this project was: can a machine learning model, trained on thousands of past patients, pick a better 20 than a nurse's rule of thumb?
Act two

Can an AI pick who to call?building it properly, then putting it to the test

First, the AI needs to see a lot of patients

A model learns from examples, so I needed lots of past patients along with what happened to each of them afterwards. I used a public research dataset of 101,766 hospital stays from 130 US hospitals between 1999 and 2008. The records are anonymous, but every one of them describes a real stay: how old the patient was, why they came in, how long they stayed, which medications changed, where they went afterwards and, most importantly, whether they were back within 30 days.

The data doesn't arrive as anything you could read, though. Each stay is one long row of codes like the one below, and the first job was turning rows like that into something both a person and a model can make sense of. Tap the cards to flip each code into plain words.

One real record, translated

So that one row is a man in his 60s with heart failure, who went home after six days with his insulin increased and was back in the hospital within the month. He had no hospital stays in the year before, but the data shows two earlier stays further back, which is the kind of history the model will learn from. Multiply him by a hundred thousand and you have the raw material for the whole project.

To make that raw material trustworthy, I loaded it into a small analytics database called DuckDB and used dbt to rebuild it as clean, linked tables for stays, patients and diagnoses. dbt also runs 35 automatic data tests on every change, so if a patient ID goes missing or an impossible value appears, the build fails loudly instead of quietly feeding bad data to the model.

Not technical? The next two boxes are the real terminal output and the real SQL, there for anyone who wants to check my work. Skip to the chart ↓

Terminal · building the data warehousedbt



  
Next I worked out each patient's history, mainly how many times they'd been in the hospital before this stay and how often those earlier stays had ended in a quick return. In SQL this is done with a window function, which lets each row look back over the same patient's earlier rows. The detail that matters most is the last line of the window: it only ever looks backwards, so the model can never peek at anything that happened after the day it's making a prediction about.




warehouse/models/marts/encounter_features.sqlSQL



  
That history turned out to be the strongest clue in the whole dataset, and it's worth seeing for yourself, because it explains the twist later on:

  
Share of patients back within 30 days
Grouped by how many earlier hospital stays the patient had in the data.

  
The more often someone has been in the hospital before, the more likely they are to come back soon, and that pattern is far stronger than anything else in the data.


  
Then, making sure the test can't flatter the model

  
With the data ready, I trained four different models, from a simple scoring rule up to XGBoost and a small neural network in PyTorch, and compared them on exactly the same patients. Training a model is the easy part these days. The harder part, and honestly the part I'm proudest of, is making sure the test can't flatter the result, and three decisions mattered far more than which algorithm won. Each one comes with the actual code, and the plain-English explanation sits right underneath it.

src/readmit/split.pyPython

    
Decision 1 · test on strangersAbout 23% of patients show up in the data more than once. If one of their stays teaches the model and another stay tests it, the model can partly recognize the person and look smarter than it really is, so every patient goes into exactly one group, decided by a fixed hash of their ID.

  

  

    
src/readmit/policy.pyPython

    
Decision 2 · plain code makes the final callThe model only produces a risk score. This short, tested function is what actually turns those scores into "today's 20," so the decision itself is a few lines that anyone can read and check.

  





  
Decision 3 was a mistake I made and then caught. My first version kept putting patients who were going to nursing homes and rehab centers at the very top of the list. The model was right that they're high-risk, since 27.7% of rehab patients came back compared with 9.3% of people who went home, but a care manager doesn't phone someone who's being looked after by a facility's own staff, so the model was answering a question nobody was asking. I limited the list to patients going home and re-ran every single test. I also removed the 2,423 stays that ended with the patient dying or entering hospice care, because counting them as "didn't come back" would teach the model that the sickest patients are the safest ones.




warehouse/models/marts/fct_encounter.sql · decision 3 in codeSQL
Reading itCodes 1, 6, 7 and 8 all mean the patient went home: on their own, with a visiting nurse, against medical advice, or with home IV treatment. Only those patients can end up on the call list.



  
The data is cleaned and tested, the model only ever learns from the past, and every result from here on comes from patients it has never seen before.

The twist: the AI mostly learned what nurses already know

  
Next to random calls, the AI looks great, because it reaches about twice as many of the people who come back. But nurses don't choose at random, and next to their simple rule, "call the people who've been in the hospital most in the past year," the AI barely moved the needle, by a gap so small that the statistics say it could easily be luck.





  
  

    
On a typical morning, 16 of the AI's 20 picks were the very same people the nurse's rule picked.

    
Remember the chart about earlier hospital stays? That clue is by far the strongest one in this data, and experienced nurses already use it, so the AI found the same clue on its own and added only a little on top of it.

  





  
I don't see that as a failure, because it's the result a hospital most needs to hear before it pays for a tool like this. Plenty of AI tools look impressive when you compare them with guessing, but the only fair test is against the people already doing the job, and here that test said the AI wasn't adding much, at least with the kind of data that's available.

  
Choosing who to call turned out not to be where AI earns its keep. So I asked a different question: what part of this job is actually slow, tedious, and easy to get wrong?








  
Act three

  
Giving the AI a better jobreading the paperwork, so the nurse doesn't have to






  
Before every single call, the nurse has to read the patient's discharge summary, which is the letter the hospital writes when someone goes home. It can run to a couple of pages of medical language, and buried somewhere in it are the three things the call is really about: which medications changed, which follow-up appointments still need to be booked, and which warning signs the patient was told to watch for.

  
Reading through that quickly and reliably is something today's language models are genuinely good at, so I built a tool that reads the summary and turns it into a short checklist for the call. The rule I cared about most is that every item on the checklist has to come with the exact sentence it was taken from, so the nurse can confirm it in a second, and if that sentence isn't really in the note, my code throws the item away. That one rule is what stops the AI from inventing a medication the patient never received. Real discharge summaries can't be shared publicly, so here it is working on a synthetic one that's written to look like the real thing:





  

    

    

  





  
Under the hood, the note is read by an open-source language model called Qwen3, running on my own graphics card through Ollama so that no patient text ever leaves the machine, and it's forced to answer in a strict JSON format. Then a few lines of plain Python check every quote against the original note before anything reaches the nurse:




src/readmit/notes/extract.pyPython



  
I checked it against 30 discharge notes that I labeled by hand. It found 28 of 28 follow-up appointments, and 9 of 11 medication changes without listing a single medication that wasn't really there. I deliberately tuned it to miss something rather than invent something, because a missed item costs one extra question on the call, while an invented drug could have a nurse asking a patient about medicine they never got.

  
The tool also suggests which clinic should follow up with the patient. For that I fine-tuned Bio_ClinicalBERT, a language model that had already been trained on clinical notes, on my own GPU in about seven minutes. On notes written in a style it had never seen before, it chose the right clinic 17 times out of 20, compared with 11 for a simpler word-counting approach.




Terminal · fine-tuning Bio_ClinicalBERT on an RTX 5070PyTorch + CUDA
Each line is one pass over the training notes. Macro-F1 is the model's average score across all 14 clinics, where 1.0 would be perfect, and it climbs from 0.31 to 0.83 as the model learns.






  
An assistant that's allowed to explain, but not to decide

  
On top of all this I built a chat assistant that a nurse or a manager can ask questions in plain English. It doesn't answer from memory. Instead it calls a handful of small tools I wrote, like "look up this patient's risk and the reasons behind it" or "read this discharge note," and it writes every step it takes to a log, so you can always see exactly how it reached an answer.

  
The more important design choice is what it's not allowed to do. It can't change who's on the call list, it can't edit any data, and if it ever mentions a patient that none of its tools actually returned, the code flags the answer. Those limits live in the code itself rather than in a polite instruction to the AI, so they hold no matter how someone phrases the question. These are real answers from its test run, next to the log entry behind the first one:





  

  
data/agent_logs · the logged run behind the first answerJSON





  
I gave it 20 test questions with answers I'd worked out from the data beforehand, including five that tried to get it to misbehave, and it got 19 of 20 right, including all five of those. The one it missed was a database query where it wrote an age group in a slightly different format from the one the data uses. Here's the guard that keeps its database tool read-only, which is just a pattern of forbidden words plus a check that the request is a single, plain question to the data:

Knowing when it quietly stops working

  
Models don't usually break loudly. They get worse quietly when the patients or the paperwork change, for example when a hospital starts recording a lab test differently. So once a month an automated GitHub Action compares the newest patients with the ones the model learned from, using a drift score, which is a single number for how different this month's patients look from the ones the model learned from. A score near 0 means nothing has changed, and anything above 0.25 means something has. The check also measures whether the call list is still reaching as many of the people who come back. If either one slips, it opens a ticket for whoever looks after the model.

  
An alarm you've never seen go off is an alarm you can't trust, so I tested it on purpose with a month I had deliberately distorted, with older patients, more previous hospital stays, and one blood test that suddenly stopped being recorded. In the normal month the bars barely move, and in the distorted month they shoot straight past the alarm line:










  
What this shows

  
How I workand the tools I used to do it






  
If I had to sum up the project in one sentence, it would be this: I built a complete AI system for a real hospital problem, tested it honestly enough to discover that the obvious use of AI wasn't the valuable one, and then moved the AI to the part of the job where it actually helps and where people can check its work. Everything on this page comes from that working code, and this is the app itself running on my machine:




The working app, recorded on my machine. It shows the day's call list, explains any patient, re-scores them live when you change a fact, and turns a discharge note into a call guide.

Getting the data right
Downloaded and checksum-verified by script, modeled as a star schema with 35 automatic data tests, and patient history built with SQL window functions.
PythonSQLDuckDBdbt

    
The risk model
Four models compared on a patient-level split, probabilities calibrated so that "23%" really means about 23 in 100, confidence intervals on every headline number, a fairness check across age, sex and race, and SHAP to turn each score into plain reasons.
scikit-learnXGBoostPyTorchSHAPMLflow

    
Reading the notes
A clinical language model fine-tuned on my GPU to suggest the right clinic, and a local LLM with strict JSON output and a quote check to build the call checklist.
Hugging FaceBio_ClinicalBERTCUDAOllamaQwen3

    
The assistant
A tool-using agent written directly on the Anthropic Messages API format, with read-only tools, a check for made-up patients, full logging, and a 20-question test that runs alongside the rest of the test suite.
Anthropic SDKtool useevaluation

    
Shipping and upkeep
A FastAPI web app in a Linux Docker container that's built and smoke-tested on every change, a PySpark version of the data build that matches the original row for row, and the monthly health check with a retraining script.

Three things I'd tell a hospital

  
Test AI against people, not just against chance. My model doubled what random calls reached, and that's the number a sales pitch would lead with, but next to a nurse's rule of thumb it added almost nothing, and only that second comparison tells you whether a tool is worth buying.

  
Getting the question right matters more than the algorithm. Testing on new patients, removing patients who died, and limiting the list to people going home decided whether the results meant anything at all, while switching between four different models moved the result by only a couple of points.

  
Put AI where people can check its work. Choosing who to call is a judgment nurses already make well, but reading a long discharge summary and quoting exactly what to confirm is tedious work where every answer can be verified in a second, and that's where the AI belongs.
